title: American Airlines 320
summary: American Airlines Flight 320, a Lockheed L-188 Electra flying from Chicago to New York, crashed into the East River about 4,900 ft short of runway 22 while approaching LaGuardia Airport through a 400 ft overcast ceiling and fog, killing 65 of 73 aboard. The Civil Aeronautics Board found the crew, new to the Electra, flew below the intended approach path while the altimeter appeared to show a safe altitude; the Air Line Pilots Association instead blamed faulty instruments. It was the first crash involving the Electra type.
probable_cause: The Civil Aeronautics Board concluded the crew made mistakes that caused the crash, with the crew's inexperience on the Electra and poor weather conditions cited as contributing factors.

events.text: The LaGuardia approach controller advised the pilots of an overcast ceiling of 400 ft and visibility of 1.25 mi, and instructed them to prepare for approach to runway 22 over the East River.
Surviving flight crew members said that, right up to the moment of impact, the altimeter had been showing they were flying a safe distance above the water.
LaGuardia tower gave the flight its final landing clearance for runway 22 when it was 2.8 mi from the airport; the crew acknowledged only with '320' and there were no further radio communications.
A witness in a car near the Whitestone Bridge saw the aircraft pass overhead only about 100 ft above the ground, lower than planes usually flew in the area.
Flying at 140 knots, the aircraft struck the East River about 4900 ft short of the runway.

notes: CAB blamed crew error/inexperience; ALPA disputed and blamed faulty instruments -- both perspectives noted
